Short paper

Reciprocal Sums and the Sylvester Recurrence

Erdős #243 By Will Cook September 2026
PDFOpen the PDF, 21 pages TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis. Every strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3) has an irrational reciprocal sum. A cubic profile for hypothetical rational-tail numerators is excluded by square specialisation and congruences modulo seven. The zero-indexed theorem has a Lean proof; the paper obtains the one-based statement by an ordinary finite-prefix argument. Separately, if 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1 and the sum is rational, an eventual upper bound on increments of 𝑃𝑛/𝑎𝑛Pn/an, with 𝑃𝑛 =∏𝑗<𝑛𝑎𝑗Pn=∏j<naj, forces the Sylvester recurrence eventually. That extra bound is not derived from growth and rationality alone; unrestricted Erdős #243 remains open.

This paper owns the cubic-rate irrationality theorem and the problem-specific exposition for Erdős #243: the centred integer state, negative-part exclusions, conditional Sylvester criterion, and remaining arithmetic estimate.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #243, which remains open.

Authorship and AI use. Will Cook built and directed the research infrastructure and maintains the public release. He reviewed claims when he could. AI agents did most of the research and drafting. Cook did not independently verify every claim.

Cite and contact. Cite this paper by its title, author and date above, with its PDF; cite the earlier sources it uses for a mathematical result. For software, use the release citation and give the commit used. Contact Will with questions or corrections.

Introduction

The Sylvester recurrence 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1 gives a rational reciprocal sum by telescoping:

1𝑎𝑛−1=1𝑎𝑛+1𝑎𝑛+1−1.1an−1=1an+1an+1−1.

For an increasing sequence of positive integers that eventually satisfies this recurrence, the tail sum at every sufficiently large index is 1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)1/(an−1). Erdős and Graham asked whether every rational reciprocal sum with 𝑎𝑛+1 ∼𝑎2𝑛an+1∼an2 arises in this way.

Problem 1.1 (Erdős Problem 243). Let 1 ≤𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯1≤a1<a2<⋯ be a sequence of integers with

lim𝑛→∞𝑎𝑛𝑎2𝑛−1=1and∑1𝑎𝑛∈ℚ.limn→∞anan−12=1and∑1an∈Q.

Then 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Erdős and Graham [5] asked this question; see also Erdős [6] and Bloom’s catalogue [11]. We prove the following irrationality result for a restricted class of sequences with 𝑎𝑛+1 ∼𝑎2𝑛an+1∼an2.

Theorem 1.2 (cubic-rate irrationality). A strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with

𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1=1+3𝑛+𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3n+o(n−3)

has irrational reciprocal sum.

Under the eventual Sylvester recurrence, 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1 =𝑂(1/𝑎𝑛)an2/an+1−1=O(1/an), which is much smaller than 3/𝑛3/n. Theorem 1.2 therefore treats a restricted case of the problem by excluding rationality altogether. The general quadratic limit 𝑎𝑛+1 ∼𝑎2𝑛an+1∼an2 remains insufficient for any argument given here.

For example, set 𝑎1 =8a1=8 and

𝑎𝑛+1=⌈𝑛𝑎2𝑛𝑛+3⌉.an+1=⌈nan2n+3⌉.

This gives 8,16,103,5305,…8,16,103,5305,…. From 𝑎𝑛+1 ≥𝑎2𝑛/4an+1≥an2/4 we obtain 𝑎𝑛 ≥4 ⋅22𝑛−1an≥4⋅22n−1 by induction. The error introduced by the ceiling is less than one, and hence

0≤1+3𝑛−𝑎2𝑛𝑎𝑛+1<16𝑎2𝑛=𝑜(𝑛−3).0≤1+3n−an2an+1<16an2=o(n−3).

The theorem applies to this explicitly defined sequence.

If the sum is rational, clearing denominators gives positive integer tail numerators 𝐶𝑛Cn. Their growth is cubic, so we compare them with 𝐹𝑛 =𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2)Fn=n(n+1)(n+2), for which 𝐹𝑛+1/𝐹𝑛 =1 +3/𝑛Fn+1/Fn=1+3/n. The ratio estimate gives 𝐶𝑛 =𝐴𝐹𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛)Cn=AFn+o(n). Subtracting the recurrences for 𝐶𝑛Cn and 𝐴𝐹𝑛AFn then shows that the first difference of the error tends to zero. It follows that Δ4𝐶𝑛 →0Δ4Cn→0. Since these fourth differences are integers, they eventually vanish, and 𝐶𝑛 =𝐴𝐹𝑛 +𝐵Cn=AFn+B.

We next use the denominator recurrence to constrain this polynomial. It gives a square condition at every root of a cubic modulo almost every prime. Chebotarev’s theorem implies that the corresponding element of the cubic number field is a square. Trace identities leave two possible polynomials; four consecutive terms modulo seven exclude both. The proof in Section 3 follows this order.

For the recurrence criteria we use the integer tail numerators of Koizumi [10]. In Section 4, a stable gcd and the Chinese remainder theorem exclude a rational tail whose quotient 𝑎1⋯𝑎𝑛−1/𝑎𝑛a1⋯an−1/an has bounded upward increments. An elementary infinite product argument gives the separate summability criterion of Section 5. We then clear the tails by a least common multiple and count crossings of new maxima (Section 6). The resulting weighted criterion isolates an arithmetic estimate still missing from the general problem. The companion paper also treats nonintegral rates and proves a stronger cubic disagreement theorem. Its detailed proof locations and the formal sources are listed in Appendix B.

Tail numerators

For the Sylvester sequence 2,3,7,43,…2,3,7,43,…, whose reciprocal sum is 11, the successive tails are 1,1/2,1/6,1/42,…1,1/2,1/6,1/42,…. Multiplication by the products 1,2,6,42,…1,2,6,42,… leaves the constant integer numerator 11. For an arbitrary rational reciprocal sum, we also multiply by a denominator of the whole sum. The resulting integer numerators need not be constant.

The integer is positive because it equals the positive tail multiplied by 𝐷𝑛Dn. Removing the term 1/𝑎𝑛1/an from the tail gives

𝐶𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛−𝐷𝑛,𝐷𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛.(1)(1)Cn+1=anCn−Dn,Dn+1=anDn.

𝑥𝑛=1𝑎𝑛+1𝑎𝑛+1+𝑂(𝑎−2𝑛+1),𝐶𝑛+1𝐶𝑛=𝑎2𝑛𝑎𝑛+1+𝑂(1/𝑎𝑛).(2)(2)xn=1an+1an+1+O(an+1−2),Cn+1Cn=an2an+1+O(1/an).

Proof of cubic-rate irrationality

Suppose, towards a contradiction, that the reciprocal sum in Theorem 1.2 is rational. Construct 𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛Cn,Dn as in Section 2. Equation (2) transfers the rate without changing its precision:

𝐶𝑛+1𝐶𝑛=1+3𝑛+𝑜(𝑛−3).(3)(3)Cn+1Cn=1+3n+o(n−3).

We first show that 𝐶𝑛Cn is eventually a polynomial, using (3) and integrality. We then apply (1) to restrict its coefficients.

This example concerns polynomial extraction alone. It is not asserted to satisfy the denominator recurrence.

Reduction and the constant term

We now use the denominator recurrence. Both updates preserve common divisors, so 𝐺𝑛 =gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Gn=gcd(Cn,Dn) forms a divisibility chain: 𝐺𝑛 ∣𝐺𝑛+1Gn∣Gn+1. For every sufficiently late 𝑛n, it divides four consecutive values of 𝐶𝑛Cn, and hence their third difference 6𝐴6A. Thus 𝐺𝑛Gn stabilises at a positive integer 𝑔g.

A square forced by a zero numerator

Let 𝛼α be a root of 𝑓f and put 𝐾 =ℚ(𝛼)K=Q(α), a cubic field. We claim that 𝛼2 −1α2−1 is a square in 𝐾K. A nonsquare would give a quadratic extension in which an automorphism fixes 𝛼α but changes the sign of its square root. Chebotarev realises this behaviour modulo a prime: the reduced 𝛼α lies in the prime field, while the square root does not. That would contradict (7).

Here are the details of this passage. Suppose 𝛼2 −1α2−1 is not a square in 𝐾K, and choose 𝛽β with 𝛽2 =𝛼2 −1β2=α2−1. The nontrivial automorphism of 𝐾(𝛽)/𝐾K(β)/K fixes 𝛼α and sends 𝛽β to −𝛽−β. Extend it to an element 𝜎 ∈Gal⁡(𝑀/ℚ)σ∈Gal⁡(M/Q), where 𝑀M is a Galois closure of 𝐾(𝛽)/ℚK(β)/Q.

Choosing a prime of 𝑀M above each of them makes the Frobenius equal to 𝜎σ itself. Omit residue characteristic two, primes dividing 6𝑚6m, and the finitely many primes where 𝛼α or 𝛽β is nonintegral or 𝛽β reduces to zero. Section 2 of the companion proves positive lower density of disagreement with each rational cubic of this form. That lower bound depends on the orbit and the cubic. For Theorem 1.2, exclusion of eventual equality suffices.

Bounded increases

We return to the rational tails of Section 2. The Sylvester example had a constant integer numerator. To measure departure from this behaviour, put

𝐸𝑛=𝐷𝑛−(𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛=𝐶𝑛−𝐶𝑛+1.En=Dn−(an−1)Cn=Cn−Cn+1.

Thus a negative error is an upward step of 𝐶𝑛Cn, and zero error says that the reciprocal tail equals 1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)1/(an−1). The next theorem forces constancy from bounded upward steps and a vanishing relative error. The latter limit already follows from quadratic growth; the bound on upward steps is an additional hypothesis. No polynomial expansion is assumed.

Theorem 4.1 (bounded negative part). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N satisfy 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1, 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, and

𝐶𝑛+1+𝐷𝑛=𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛(𝑛≥0).Cn+1+Dn=anCn,Dn+1=anDn(n≥0).

Put 𝐸𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛En=Dn−(an−1)Cn. If

𝐸𝑛𝐶𝑛⟶0and𝐸𝑛≥−𝐵for all sufficiently large 𝑛EnCn⟶0andEn≥−Bfor all sufficiently large n

for some integer 𝐵 ≥0B≥0, then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

The relative limit is equivalently the assertion that, for every 𝐾 ∈ℕK∈N, we eventually have 𝐾|𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛K|En|<Cn. This is the division-free form used in the linked theorem. The case 𝐾 =1K=1 lets us propagate a zero error. In the absence of late zeros, the same limit and integrality force 𝐶𝑛 →∞Cn→∞. We shall then use the bound on upward steps to stabilise the gcd and produce a block of consecutive integers that the numerator cannot cross.

Proposition 4.2 (error identities). For integer sequences satisfying (1),

𝐶𝑛+1=𝐶𝑛−𝐸𝑛,(𝑎𝑛+1−𝑎2𝑛+𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛+1=𝑎2𝑛𝐸𝑛−𝐸𝑛+1.Cn+1=Cn−En,(an+1−an2+an−1)Cn+1=an2En−En+1.

Theorem 4.3 (absorption and descent). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N satisfy 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1, 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0 and (1). If |𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛|En|<Cn for every 𝑛n, then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 implies 𝐸𝑛+1 =0En+1=0. A stable gcd and a forbidden block

Proposition 4.5 (gcd stabilisation). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N satisfy 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1, 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0 and (1). For this gcd argument, bounded negative errors need occur only arbitrarily late. To control the first crossing below, we shall need the upper bound on every sufficiently late upward step.

A sequence avoiding multiples of 22 and 33 cannot cross the pair 6𝑘 +2,6𝑘 +36k+2,6k+3 from below with upward steps at most two: its first value at least 6𝑘 +26k+2 would be one of those two integers. Decreases before that crossing do not help. For a general step bound 𝐵B, the Chinese remainder theorem supplies a forbidden block of length 𝐵B.

Lemma 4.6 (consecutive multiples). For pairwise coprime integers 𝑚0,…,𝑚𝐵−1 ≥2m0,…,mB−1≥2 and every lower bound, there is a larger 𝑡t such that 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑡 +𝑖mi∣t+i for each 𝑖 <𝐵i<B.

𝑡≤𝑢𝑛≤𝑢𝑛−1+𝐵<𝑡+𝐵.t≤un≤un−1+B<t+B.

Thus 𝑢𝑛 =𝑡 +𝑖un=t+i for some 𝑖 <𝐵 <𝑛i<B<n, and 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑢𝑛mi∣un, contrary to gcd(𝑚𝑖,𝑢𝑛) =1gcd(mi,un)=1. ◻

Finite total relative increase

An infinite product gives another way to bound a numerator. This argument needs only the scalar update 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 −𝐸𝑛Cn+1=Cn−En and positivity on a discrete set. We assume summability of the relative upward increments. Mere convergence of those increments to zero would allow 𝐶𝑛 =𝑛 +1Cn=n+1 and 𝐶𝑛 =(𝑛 +1)2Cn=(n+1)2, both of which grow without bound.

Theorem 5.1 (a convergent sum of relative increases). Let 𝐶𝑛Cn be positive integers and 𝐸𝑛En integers satisfying 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 −𝐸𝑛Cn+1=Cn−En. If

∑𝑛(−𝐸𝑛)+𝐶𝑛<∞,∑n(−En)+Cn<∞,

then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 eventually. Neither denominator dynamics nor vanishing relative error is required.

Proof. Set 𝛿𝑛 =( −𝐸𝑛)+/𝐶𝑛δn=(−En)+/Cn. Then

𝐶𝑁≤𝐶0∏𝑛<𝑁(1+𝛿𝑛)≤𝐶0exp(∑𝑛𝛿𝑛).CN≤C0∏n<N(1+δn)≤C0exp(∑nδn).

Choose an integer 𝐾K above this bound. A strict rise of the integer sequence has size at least one, so it contributes at least 1/𝐾1/K to ∑𝛿𝑛∑δn. Hence only finitely many rises occur. Thereafter 𝐶𝑛Cn is a nonincreasing positive integer sequence, and its eventual constancy gives 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0. ◻

The proof also allows positive real 𝐶𝑛Cn with integer 𝐸𝑛En: the values lie in 𝐶0 +ℤC0+Z, whose bounded positive part is finite. Discrete increments are essential to this argument. With real errors, 𝐶𝑛 =1 +1/(𝑛 +1)Cn=1+1/(n+1) decreases forever with zero relative-increase sum; without positivity, 𝐶𝑛 = −𝑛 −1Cn=−n−1, 𝐸𝑛 =1En=1 does so too. The companion’s Section 13 gives the details.

On an exact reciprocal-tail orbit the conclusion gives the Sylvester recurrence. For the gap sequence of the pseudo-greedy expansion, the same criterion, with the same product bound and integer descent, appears in the Erdős Problem a Day working report on Problem #243, dated 12 August 2026 [8]; the statement above is for any positive integer sequence with 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 −𝐸𝑛Cn+1=Cn−En. This summability condition and the bound in Theorem 4.1 are different estimates. For exact reciprocal tails with |𝐸𝑛|/𝐶𝑛 →0|En|/Cn→0, each is equivalent to eventual vanishing of 𝐸𝑛En; neither estimate has been derived here from the unrestricted problem.

Corollary 6.2 (a bound using the least common multiple). Assume the hypotheses of Problem 1.1. Write 𝐴𝑛 =lcm⁡(𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛−1)An=lcm⁡(a1,…,an−1) with 𝐴1 =1A1=1. If

lim sup𝑛→∞𝐴𝑛𝑎𝑛(𝑎2𝑛𝑎𝑛+1−1)<∞,lim supn→∞Anan(an2an+1−1)<∞,

Proof. Since 𝐿𝑛/𝐴𝑛 =𝑞/gcd(𝑞,𝐴𝑛)Ln/An=q/gcd(q,An) lies in [1,𝑞][1,q], an upper bound on the expression in the corollary gives an upper bound on (𝐿𝑛/𝑎𝑛)(𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1)(Ln/an)(an2/an+1−1); negative terms remain negative. Equation (10) therefore bounds the negative part of 𝑉𝑛Vn. Choose an integer 𝐵B above that eventual bound. The record series then vanishes after a finite prefix, so Theorem 6.1 applies. ◻

The expression in Erdős and Straus’s Theorem 3 is

[𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑘]𝑎𝑘+1(𝑎2𝑘+1𝑎𝑘+2−1),[a1,…,ak]ak+1(ak+12ak+2−1),

with a nonpositive upper limit [1]. Setting 𝑛 =𝑘 +1n=k+1 gives exactly (𝐴𝑛/𝑎𝑛)𝛾𝑛(An/an)γn: the prefix ends before 𝑎𝑛an, and the growth ratio begins at 𝑎𝑛an. Tijdeman and Yuan extend this type of criterion to positive numerators [4]. Here any finite upper bound suffices under the quadratic-limit assumption. Since 𝐴𝑛 ∣𝑃𝑛An∣Pn, the LCM hypothesis is no stronger than the product hypothesis in Corollary 4.9: if the product expression is at most 𝐵B, the LCM expression is at most max(𝐵,0)max(B,0). When the earlier terms are pairwise coprime the two weights agree; repeated prime factors can make the LCM much smaller. This comparison does not assert the existence of a non-Sylvester rational example satisfying one bound but not the other.

The finite upper limit means an eventual upper bound; it does not require 𝑞q to divide the LCM of the preceding denominators. For positive integer summand numerators 𝑏𝑛bn, the modified error is 𝑉𝑛 =𝑏𝑛𝐿𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝑈𝑛Vn=bnLn−(an−1)Un. The companion, Section 6 under “Integer coefficients”, separately proves boundedness from a lower bound on 𝑉𝑛Vn and eventual constancy when 𝑉𝑛/𝑈𝑛 →0Vn/Un→0 is also assumed. The latter conclusion must not be read into the first hypothesis alone. The same section links finite examples separating them; compare Badea [3] and Tijdeman–Yuan [4]. The companion’s Section 3 compares Duverney’s signed-series criterion [2], whose printed condition is one-sided, with the stronger absolute-convergence specialisation used there. It also records the different growth hypotheses for irrationality exponents in [14]. Neither comparison is an input to the crossing theorem.

Proposition 7.1 (necessary profile). The integer tail of a sequence satisfying Problem 1.1’s hypotheses but not its conclusion has 𝐸𝑛 ≠0En≠0 eventually, |𝐸𝑛|/𝐶𝑛 →0|En|/Cn→0, unbounded negative magnitudes along negative indices, and

∑𝑛(−𝐸𝑛)+𝐶𝑛=∞.∑n(−En)+Cn=∞.

The weighted criterion reduces the problem to a statement about this cumulative sum. We would need to show, from growth and rationality, that for some fixed integer 𝐵 ≥0B≥0,

lim inf𝑋→∞𝐹𝐵(𝑋)𝑋=0.(13)(13)lim infX→∞FB(X)X=0.

If the recurrence is not eventually Sylvester, first crossings instead give 𝐹𝐵(𝑋) ≥𝑋/𝑃𝐵 −𝑂𝐵(1)FB(X)≥X/PB−OB(1), with an orbit-dependent CRT modulus 𝑃𝐵PB. The sum groups each record step by its starting numerator 𝑈𝑛Un, not by the running maximum 𝑅𝑛Rn or the time index. If the eventual Sylvester recurrence fails, 𝑈𝑛 →∞Un→∞, so only finitely many of these steps begin below any fixed 𝑋X. To see the equivalence with an admissible weight, enumerate the record indices by 𝑗j and apply the next lemma with 𝑢𝑗 =𝑈𝑛uj=Un and 𝑤𝑗 =( −𝑉𝑛 −𝐵)+wj=(−Vn−B)+. The lemma supplies a weight once (13) holds. Establishing that estimate would contradict the first-crossing lower bound and exclude every non-Sylvester rational tail.

Lemma 7.2 (weights and linear density). Let 𝑢𝑗uj be positive integers, let 𝑤𝑗 ≥0wj≥0, and put 𝐹(𝑋) =∑𝑢𝑗≤𝑋𝑤𝑗F(X)=∑uj≤Xwj, with the sum allowed a priori to be +∞+∞. Then lim inf𝑋→∞𝐹(𝑋)/𝑋 =0lim infX→∞F(X)/X=0 if and only if there is a finite nonincreasing 𝑓 :[1,∞) →[0,∞)f:[1,∞)→[0,∞) with ∫∞1𝑓(𝑡) 𝑑𝑡 =∞∫1∞f(t)dt=∞ and ∑𝑗𝑤𝑗𝑓(𝑢𝑗) <∞∑jwjf(uj)<∞.

𝑓(𝑡)=∑𝑘≥1𝟏[1,𝑋𝑘](𝑡)𝑋𝑘.f(t)=∑k≥11[1,Xk](t)Xk.

Arithmetic compatibility

The remaining estimate requires the denominator recurrence as well as control of the error. For example, 𝐶𝑛 =𝑛2 +1Cn=n2+1, 𝐸𝑛 = −(2𝑛 +1)En=−(2n+1) has vanishing relative error and the necessary scalar pattern. But at 𝑛 =2,3,4n=2,3,4 its numerators are 5,10,175,10,17. The update 10 =5𝑎2 −𝐷210=5a2−D2 forces 5 ∣𝐷25∣D2, hence 5 ∣𝐷3 =𝑎2𝐷25∣D3=a2D2; the next update would force 5 ∣175∣17. Thus these numerators cannot satisfy (1). The companion’s Section 14 also constructs sequences avoiding sparse fixed moduli and distinguishes that avoidance from compatibility with all later denominators. Neither property alone supplies (13).

Conversely, suppose integer sequences indexed from zero satisfy (1), with 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1, 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, 𝐷𝑛 ≥0Dn≥0 and 𝐸𝑛/𝐶𝑛 →0En/Cn→0. Section 4 of the companion proves that 𝐷𝑛 >0Dn>0, 𝐶𝑛/𝐷𝑛 →0Cn/Dn→0, ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛 =𝐶0/𝐷0∑n1/an=C0/D0 and 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1. All these hypotheses concern the infinite sequences; a scalar example or a finite initial segment satisfies only some of them.

Problem 7.3 (growth of repeated denominator factors). For every rational-tail orbit satisfying the hypotheses but not the conclusion of Problem 1.1, must

lim sup𝑛→∞log⁡𝑀𝑛𝑛>0?lim supn→∞log⁡Mnn>0?

Equivalently, must there be a 𝐾 ≥1K≥1 for which

2𝑛≤𝑀𝐾𝑛2n≤MnK

at infinitely many indices?

Section 2 gives 𝐶𝑛+1/𝐶𝑛 →1Cn+1/Cn→1; averaging logarithms therefore gives log⁡𝐶𝑛 =𝑜(𝑛)log⁡Cn=o(n). Since 1 ≤𝑀𝑛 ≤𝐶𝑛1≤Mn≤Cn, every such orbit already satisfies log⁡𝑀𝑛/𝑛 →0log⁡Mn/n→0. A positive answer therefore holds exactly when no such orbit exists: proving it from failure of Sylvester behaviour would exclude every counterexample.

A factorial modulus for integral recursion

A constant-negative error 𝐸𝑛 = −𝑚En=−m with 𝐶0 =𝑐C0=c gives 𝐶𝑛 =𝑐 +𝑛𝑚Cn=c+nm and the identity

𝐷𝑛+𝑚=(𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛.(14)(14)Dn+m=(an−1)Cn.

In the case 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1, where (14) reads 𝐷𝑛 +1 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)(𝑛 +1)Dn+1=(an−1)(n+1), each multiplier is determined by its predecessor. The recursion is 𝑎𝑛+1 =num⁡(𝑛,𝑎𝑛)/(𝑛 +2)an+1=num⁡(n,an)/(n+2), where

num⁡(𝑛,𝑎)=(𝑛+1)𝑎2−(𝑛+2)𝑎+(𝑛+3),num⁡(n,a)=(n+1)a2−(n+2)a+(n+3),

the forced numerator. We stop at the first nonintegral quotient. This procedure checks divisibility only; it does not impose the positivity conditions required of an infinite reciprocal-tail sequence. The formal exact-division condition requires exact division at each step.

Example A.1 (a nonintegral second step). Starting from 𝑎0 =3a0=3, the first numerator num⁡(0,3) =6num⁡(0,3)=6 is divisible by 22, giving 𝑎1 =3a1=3. The next numerator num⁡(1,3) =13num⁡(1,3)=13 is not divisible by 33, so the recursion stops.

Direct iteration can produce very large intermediate integers. To decide whether the first ℎh divisions are exact, however, it suffices to know the initial value modulo (ℎ +1)!(h+1)!. Computing a pseudo-greedy orbit through residues modulo a shrinking product modulus is Koizumi’s method [10]; for the forced numerator that product is a factorial.

Theorem A.2 (factorial residue reduction). Let ℎh be a nonnegative integer and let 𝑎,𝑏a,b be integers with 𝑎 ≡𝑏(mod(ℎ +1)!)a≡b(mod(h+1)!). The first ℎh steps of the recursion 𝑎𝑛+1 =num⁡(𝑛,𝑎𝑛)/(𝑛 +2)an+1=num⁡(n,an)/(n+2), starting at index zero, are integral for 𝑎0 =𝑎a0=a if and only if they are integral for 𝑎0 =𝑏a0=b.

Proof. Define 𝑀(0,𝑖) =1M(0,i)=1 and 𝑀(ℎ +1,𝑖) =(𝑖 +2)𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h+1,i)=(i+2)M(h,i+1). Thus 𝑀(ℎ,0) =(ℎ +1)!M(h,0)=(h+1)!. We prove the stronger statement that, at index 𝑖i, congruent inputs modulo 𝑀(ℎ,𝑖)M(h,i) give the same answer to whether the next ℎh quotients are all integral. There is nothing to prove for ℎ =0h=0.

For the inductive step, suppose 𝑎 ≡𝑏(mod(𝑖 +2)𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1))a≡b(mod(i+2)M(h,i+1)). Since num⁡(𝑖, ⋅)num⁡(i,⋅) is an integer polynomial, its values at 𝑎a and 𝑏b are congruent modulo that product. In particular, one is divisible by 𝑖 +2i+2 if and only if the other is. If neither is divisible, both recursions stop. Otherwise their quotients are congruent modulo 𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h,i+1), so the induction hypothesis applies to the remaining ℎh updates at index 𝑖 +1i+1. Taking 𝑖 =0i=0 proves the claim. ◻

For ℎ =1h=1, the condition is 2 ∣𝑎2 −2𝑎 +32∣a2−2a+3, or equivalently that 𝑎a is odd. This illustrates Theorem A.2 with modulus 2! =22!=2.

The enumeration in Example 9.1 of the companion, over 2 ≤𝑎0 <50002≤a0<5000, gives at most 1717 successful updates (1818 values including 𝑎0a0). The seed 𝑎0 =1a0=1 is excluded because it is fixed and violates 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2. This finite calculation establishes only the stated range. The infinite constant-negative exclusion requires the separate argument under the hypotheses given there.

Sources and related work

The companion Reciprocal Sums and the Sylvester Recurrence: Further Results and Proofs gives full proofs and fixed-revision source links. Section 2 treats regular rates and the stronger cubic disagreement result; Sections 4–5 develop the integer tail numerators. The gcd and bounded-increment arguments culminate in Section 12. The LCM results are in Section 6, scalar summability in Section 13, and open estimates and failed constructions in Section 14. A final map records the dependencies. The auxiliary constructions need not be rational reciprocal series; they satisfy only the hypotheses stated for them.

The older integer-remainder method is represented by Erdős–Straus [12]. The polynomial Cantor-series hypotheses in Hančl–Tijdeman [13] and the freely selectable series of Problem #270 [15] concern different settings; the companion’s Section 3 explains the distinction. The Isabelle/HOL work [16] formalises older Erdős–Straus criteria, not Problem #243. The general regular-rate extraction in the companion also uses the standard Gamma-ratio asymptotics recorded in [17]; the cubic specialisation here uses only its explicit polynomial 𝐹𝑛Fn.

Indexing of the canonical tails.

The construction in Section 2 has 𝐶1 =𝑝C1=p, 𝐷1 =𝑞D1=q. For a zero-based recurrence orbit, set 𝑎0 =1a0=1, 𝐷0 =𝑞D0=q and 𝐶0 =𝑝 +𝑞C0=p+q; one update gives those initial values. This extends the two recurrences, but supplies neither 𝑎0 >1a0>1 nor strict increase at that first step. For the zero-based strictly increasing sequence in the formal cubic theorem, instead choose 𝑁N with 𝑎𝑁 >𝑁aN>N and put 𝑏𝑛 =𝑛 +1bn=n+1 for 0 ≤𝑛 <𝑁0≤n<N, 𝑏𝑛 =𝑎𝑛bn=an for 𝑛 ≥𝑁n≥N. Then (𝑏𝑛)(bn) is strictly increasing, its reciprocal sum differs from the original sum by a rational finite sum, and its rate has the same index 𝑛n after 𝑁N. In particular, no shift of 3/𝑛3/n is made. The companion’s indexing subsection gives this finite-prefix bridge.

Verification and reproducibility

The links identify fixed-revision Lean declarations and recorded Comparator checks. The printed cubic argument uses Chebotarev; the formal square-specialisation proof uses a Dedekind-zeta pole comparison. Their common conclusion does not check each step of the printed proof. This revision includes no new Lean build, Comparator replay or independent review. The evidence record retains source-pin and index gaps, and the estimate in Section 7 remains open.

The formal factorial residue reduction uses the shrinking-modulus induction, polynomial congruence, and cancellation after exact division. Its modulus is identified by the ascending-factorial formula and its factorial value at the initial index.
